It may seem strange that Daniel was not first summoned. But it was ordered by God's providence that he should be reserved to the last, in order that all mere human means should be proved vain, before God manifested His power through His servant; thus the haughty king was stripped of all fleshly confidences. Compare as to their watchfulness, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.8">Re 4:8</reference>, "full of eyes within ... they rest not day and night." Also they watch good men committed to their charge (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.7">Psa 34:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.14">He 1:14</reference>); and watch over the evil to record their sins, and at God's bidding at last punish them (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.16">Jr 4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.17">17</reference>), "watchers" applied to human instruments of God's vengeance. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12023"/><div sID="gen21726" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12023"/><hi type="bold">17. demand--</hi>that is, determination; namely, as to the change to which Nebuchadnezzar is to be doomed. A solemn council of the heavenly ones is supposed (compare <reference osisRef="Job.1.6">Job 1:6</reference>; 2:1), over which God presides supreme. His "decree" and "word" are therefore said to be theirs (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.4.24">Da 4:24</reference>, "decree of the Most High"); "the decree of the watchers," "the word of the holy ones." For He has placed particular kingdoms under the administration of angelic beings, subject to Him (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">Da 10:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">12:1</reference>). The word "demand," in the second clause, expresses a distinct idea from the first clause. Not only as members of God's council (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.10">Da 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.19">1Ki 22:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.21">Psa 103:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.1.10">Zec 1:10</reference>) do they subscribe to His "decree," but that decree is in answer to their prayers, wherein they demand that every mortal who tries to obscure the glory of God shall be humbled [Calvin]. Angels are grieved when God's prerogative is in the least infringed. How awful to Nebuchadnezzar to know that angels plead against him for his pride, and that the decree has been passed in the high court of heaven for his humiliation in answer to angels' demands! The conceptions are moulded in a form peculiarly adapted to Nebuchadnezzar's modes of thought.<div eID="gen21726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the living--</hi>not as distinguished from the dead, but from the inhabitants of heaven, who "know" that which the men of the world need to the taught (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.16">Psa 9:16</reference>); the ungodly confess there is a God, but would gladly confine Him to heaven. But, saith Daniel, God ruleth not merely there, but "in the kingdom of men."<div eID="gen21727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21728" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">basest--</hi>the lowest in condition (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.8">1Sa 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.52">Lu 1:52</reference>). It is not one's talents, excellency, or noble birth, but God's will, which elevates to the throne. Nebuchadnezzar abased to the dunghill, and then restored, was to have in himself an experimental proof of this (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.37">Da 4:37</reference>). <div eID="gen21728" type="x-p"/>

Babylon, that I have built--</hi>Herodotus ascribes the building of Babylon to Semiramis and Nitocris, his informant under the Persian dynasty giving him the Assyrian and Persian account. Berosus and Abydenus give the Babylonian account, namely, that Nebuchadnezzar added much to the old city, built a splendid palace and city walls. Herodotus, the so-called "father of history," does not even mention Nebuchadnezzar. (Nitocris, to whom he attributes the beautifying of Babylon, seems to have been Nebuchadnezzar's wife). Hence infidels have doubted the Scripture account. But the latter is proved by thousands of bricks on the plain, the inscriptions of which have been deciphered, each marked "Nebuchadnezzar, the son of Nabopolassar." "Built," that is, restored and enlarged (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.5">2Ch 11:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.6">6</reference>). It is curious, all the bricks have been found with the stamped face downwards. Scarcely a figure in stone, or tablet, has been dug out of the rubbish heaps of Babylon, whereas Nineveh abounds in them; fulfilling <reference osisRef="Jer.51.37">Jr 51:37</reference>, "Babylon shall become heaps." The "I" is emphatic, by which he puts himself in the place of God; so the "my ... my." He impiously opposes his might to God's, as though God's threat, uttered a year before, could never come to pass. He would be more than man; God, therefore, justly, makes him less than man.
